Linear homogeneous DE of order n with constant coefficients
Now we will consider linear homogeneous differential equation of order n with constant coefficients

                   L(y) ≡y (n)(x) + a1y (n−1)(x) + ... + an−1y ′(x) + any(x) = 0,                  (1)

where a1, ..., an are real constants. We would like to solve (1) by trying an exponential exp(λx). We see
that
         d                     d2                        dn
            exp(λx) = λ exp(λx),     exp(λx) = λ2 exp(λx), ...,     exp(λx) = λn exp(λx).
         dx                     dx2                        dxn
Then
           L(exp(λx)) = λn exp(λx) + a1λn−1 exp(λx) + ... + an−1λ exp(λx) + an exp(λx)
                = (λn + a1λn−1 + ... + an−1λ + an) exp(λx)

and hence
                                  L(exp(λx)) = p(λ) exp(λx),                                  (2)





Alexander Gladkov, Professor  (Belarusian State University)                 DIFFERENTIAL EQUATIONS                                  September 15, 2026                 3 / 43

where
                            p(λ) = λn + a1λn−1 + ... + an−1λ + an.                             (3)

We call p(λ) the characteristic polynomial of L. Since exp(λx) ̸= 0, we obtain that if exp(λx) is a
solution of (1) then the constant λ must satisfy the equation p(λ) = 0 or

                             λn + a1λn−1 + a2λn−2 + ... + an = 0.                              (4)

This equation is called the characteristic equation of the given differential equation (1). Hence, to solve
(1), we write the characteristic equation (4) and solve it for λ. Observe that (4) is formally obtained
from (1) by merely replacing the k-th derivative in (1) by λk (k = 0, 1, 2, ..., n).
             ..................................................................................................................................
We need some information from algebra.
DEFINITION 1.
We say that polynomial p(λ) has a root λ1 if

                                    p(λ) = (λ −λ1)q(λ)                                      (5)

and q(λ) is another polynomial.




Alexander Gladkov, Professor  (Belarusian State University)                 DIFFERENTIAL EQUATIONS                                  September 15, 2026                 4 / 43

DEFINITION 2.
We say that a root λ1 of polynomial p(λ) has multiplicity m1 if

                                   p(λ) = (λ −λ1)m1q(λ)                                     (6)

and q(λ) is a such polynomial that q(λ1) ̸= 0.
EXAMPLE.
Let us consider polynomial
                                   p(λ) = λ3 −λ2 −λ + 1.

It is not difficult to check that

                p(λ) = λ2(λ −1) −(λ −1) = (λ2 −1)(λ −1) = (λ −1)2(λ + 1).

The root λ1 = 1 of polynomial p(λ) has multiplicity 2 and the root λ2 = −1 of polynomial p(λ) has
multiplicity 1.
From the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra we know that a polynomial of degree n always has n
complex roots (including multiplicity). Some or all roots may be real.
For conjugate to z complex number we use notation z. If z = a + ib then z = a −ib. Here i is
imaginary unit, i2 = −1.



Alexander Gladkov, Professor  (Belarusian State University)                 DIFFERENTIAL EQUATIONS                                  September 15, 2026                 5 / 43

The complex conjugate root theorem states that if p is a polynomial in one variable with real
coefficients, and a + ib is a root of p with a and b real numbers (b ̸= 0 ), then its complex conjugate
a −ib is also a root of p.
Moreover, if a + ib is the root of multiplicity k, then its complex conjugate a −ib is also the root of the
same multiplicity k.

EXAMPLE.
Let us consider polynomial
                                    p(λ) = λ4 + 2λ2 + 1.

It is not difficult to check that

               p(λ) = (λ2 + 1)2 = (λ2 −i2)2 = [(λ + i)(λ −i)]2 = (λ −i)2(λ + i)2.

The polynomial p(λ) has complex conjugate roots λ1 = i and λ2 = −i of multiplicity 2.

To solve linear homogeneous differential equation of order n we need find the roots of polynomial of the
same order. There is a simple test to find rational roots for polynomial with integer coefficients.
THEOREM 3.
If a polynomial with integer coefficients

                      P(x) = a0xn + a1xn−1 + a2xn−2 + ... + an−1x + an

has a rational root x0 = p/q (p/q is not cancellable fraction) then the number q is a divisor of the
number a0, and the number p is a divisor of the number an.
Proof. Indeed, since x0 = p/q is a root of the polynomial P(x) then

                   p  n      p  n−1      p  n−2            p
                   a0    + a1     + a2     + ... + an−1   + an = 0.
                   q         q           q                 q

Multiplying both sides of this equation by qn, we obtain

                     a0pn + a1pn−1q + a2pn−2q2 + ... + an−1pqn−1 + anqn = 0





Alexander Gladkov, Professor  (Belarusian State University)                 DIFFERENTIAL EQUATIONS                                  September 15, 2026                14 / 43

or
                    a0pn = −q(a1pn−1 + a2pn−2q + ... + an−1pqn−2 + anqn−1).

Since a0, a1, ..., an−1, an are integers, then the number in brackets is an integer. Hence, the right-hand
side of this equality is divided by q, since q is included in it as a factor. This means that the left-hand
side is divided by q. The numbers p and q as well as pn and q do not have a common factors, since
otherwise the fraction p/q would be cancellable. Hence a0 is divided by q.
Considering the equation

                   anqn = −p(a0pn−1 + a1pn−2q + a2pn−3q2 + ... + an−1qn−1),

we can prove in a similar way that an is divided by p.
